title: Toward a novel framework of understanding the relationship between social media use and political knowledge: a systematic literature review
authors: Cato Waeterloos, Desiree Schmuck, Peter Van Aelst, Michaël Opgenhaffen
abstract: While recent quantitative research finds little evidence that citizens learn about politics from social media, it is unclear whether studies adequately capture platform complexity and often fragmented understandings of political knowledge. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically reviewed 78 papers that assess the quantitative association between social media use and political knowledge. Our critical assessment of how such studies conceptualize and operationalize social media use and political knowledge revealed a dual mismatch. First, social media use is often measured via general frequency, overlooking specific content (beyond “news”), actors (e.g., influencers), platforms (beyond Facebook/Twitter), and exposure modes (e.g., incidental). Second, knowledge measures remain conservative, focusing on institutional facts while neglecting issue-specific and noninstitutional topics. We propose a novel 3-dimensional framework and methodological pathways to address key limitations in the dominant normative tradition of studying the relationship between social media and political learning.
journal_full: Annals of the International Communication Association

title: Parent–Child Play and Media Addiction in Adolescence: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study
authors: Chaeyun Lee, Hye In Jeong, Yeolib Kim
abstract: Although media addiction is a recognized public health concern, the theoretical framework surrounding its longitudinal development remains relatively underdeveloped. This study addresses that gap by evaluating a developmental model that traces a path from early parent–child play at age 6 to adolescent media addiction at age 14, with executive function and peer attachment at age 10 examined as parallel mediators. We used three waves of data from a representative sample of 1,130 parent–child dyads in the Panel Study on Korean Children. Early parent–child play at age 6 significantly predicted higher executive function at age 10, which subsequently predicted lower media addiction at age 14. This indirect path via executive function was statistically significant. Conversely, the indirect effect through peer attachment was not significant, as peer attachment was unrelated to both early play and subsequent media addiction. The direct effect of parent–child play on adolescent media addiction was nonsignificant, demonstrating that the protective influence of early family play operates through cognitive mechanisms rather than social bonds. These findings shift the clinical focus from proximal adolescent factors to early prevention, emphasizing middle childhood as a critical therapeutic window for bolstering executive function to mitigate later media addiction risks.

title: Writing the Situated Self: Intersectional and Geographic Patterning in College Admissions Essays
authors: AJ Alvero, anthony lising antonio, Leslie Luqueño, Francis Pearman
abstract: Written language is often considered a reflection of the author's internal thoughts, states, and characteristics. This is why writing is used in evaluation to make inferences about authors, but also why social scientists use text as a lens into psychological states. We present a complementary perspective: that writing systematically reflects the social environments of authors. We explore these dynamics in a large corpus of college admissions essays ( n = 232,838 essays submitted by 76,510 self-identified Hispanic applicants from 2015 to 2017) and metadata about author sociodemographics, including the ZIP code of their high school, gender identity, and household income. We find that intersectional demographic markers are highly salient. We further demonstrate that ZIP code-level socioeconomic measures are strongly correlated with the writing style and content of local applicants. Finally, we show that misclassification rates vary geographically and are modestly associated with local demographic composition and social capital, indicating that writing is influenced both socially and geographically. By documenting strong alignment between text and authors that is observable through machine reading, our findings clarify how author demographics and context structure what is written and, stylistically, how. Framing text as an external, social process rather than purely internal creates opportunities to bridge psychological and sociological data, methods, and theories to better understand the connections between language and society, especially in moments of evaluation. Because these texts were produced before the popularization of large language models (LLMs), our results serve as useful benchmarks for archival work and also generate new questions as LLMs mediate written self-presentation.
journal_full: Journal of Language and Social Psychology

title: Explaining Science Knowledge Gaps on Social Media: Basic Science Knowledge and Intentional Versus Incidental Exposure
authors: Wenbo Li, Christine Gilbert, Shan Xu
abstract: This study examined whether basic science knowledge helps explain education-based gaps in domain-specific science knowledge and whether intentional and incidental exposure on social media condition those gaps. A national survey of American adults focused on two domains: climate change and algorithms. Results showed that basic science knowledge mediated the relationship between education and domain-specific knowledge across both domains. These indirect relationship were attenuated at higher levels of intentional social media exposure. The findings suggest that strengthening foundational science literacy and encouraging more deliberate engagement with science content on social media may help reduce knowledge disparities.

title: mlstats : An R Package for Multilevel Descriptive Statistics and Data Preparation
authors: Felix Dietrich
abstract: Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats , an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics—including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations—in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on Comprehensive R Archive Network with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/ .

title: Feelings among friends and foes in populist communication: The Finns Party leadership’s emotional appeals on social media during the 2023 Finnish parliamentary election
authors: Jesper Eklund, Jon Järviniemi
abstract: This study examines the use of emotional appeals in the social media communication by members of the populist radical right Finns Party leadership during the 2023 Finnish parliamentary election campaign. While previous research has highlighted the importance of emotions in populist communication, less empirical attention has been devoted to how populist radical right actors employ both negative and positive emotional appeals, how these appeals are directed toward different targets, and how their use varies across social media platforms. To address these gaps, we conducted a quantitative content analysis of 524 social media posts published on X (Twitter), TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram by six members of the Finns Party leadership. The findings show that negative emotional appeals are more prevalent and are primarily directed toward “elites” and “dangerous outgroups”, reinforcing a negative collective identity construction of antagonistic “others”. In contrast, positive emotional appeals are also used extensively and are primarily directed toward “the people” and populist actors as their representatives, reinforcing a positive collective identity construction of “us”. Finally, the analysis reveals variation across platforms, highlighting the need for further research on the relationship between social media platforms and emotional appeals.

title: Vaccine framing dynamics: Media influence, social media sharing, and public sensemaking during a crisis
authors: Austin Y. Hubner
abstract: During crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, information dissemination and sensemaking processes profoundly shape public perceptions. This study investigates the intricate interplay between media framing, social media sharing, and individual reinterpretation of COVID-19 vaccination news on Facebook. Analyzing 1957 articles from The New York Times (NYT) over 2 years, the research delves into news framing dynamics and their influence on Facebook sharing patterns. Findings reveal eight frames used by journalists, with a focus on scientific development, political controversy, and societal impact. Notably, the anti-vaccination frame received the highest number of shares per article. I also explored the content of the individual shares examining how individuals changed the information provided by the NYT during the sharing process.

title: Identifying Alternatives to Retraction of Controversial Research Findings
authors: Mitch Brown, Donald F. Sacco, August Namuth, Cory J. Clark, Nathan Honeycutt
abstract: Although academic journals have historically prioritized dissemination of accurate information, some journals now consider information hazards in editorial policies. Editors may reject or retract papers based on their perceived potential to impose societal harms. Such editorial policies have received pushback from scholars seeing such policies as impediments to effective science communication. Across four experiments, we tested how both scientists and everyday people view harm-based retractions and alternatives to retraction for addressing controversy. Academic researchers and lay perceivers disapproved of retractions based on information hazards, preferring commentaries, replications, adversarial collaborations, and even inaction . We offer policy recommendations for science communication.

title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-Being on Instagram
authors: Gregory John Depow, Christopher Oveis, Emily Zohar, Michael Inzlicht
abstract: Two-thirds of the global population spends significant time browsing social media, making it critical to understand how to improve online experiences to support well-being. Social media use is often linked to both positive and negative psychological outcomes, but interventions to enhance well-being during social media use remain limited. Here, we test whether an intervention embedded in daily life that trains individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. Drawing from strategic regulation of empathy and wisdom, we used an ecological momentary intervention to train half our sample ( N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative emotions on their own Instagram feeds. Using experience sampling ( N obs . = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online – boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing and compassion for negative emotions – while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons and personal distress. On surveys where participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media by helping users engage more adaptively with emotional content. This work extends our understanding of how empathy predicts well-being and elucidates the relationship between social media use and well-being, with broad societal implications for our increasingly digital society.

title: Scrolling for the Truth: Source Factors, Persuasion, and a Test of Misinformation Interventions on TikTok
authors: Brittany N. Shivers Weinstein, Bartosz W. Wojdynski
abstract: The popularity of the video-based social media platform TikTok has rapidly grown in recent years, and with it its role in rapidly disseminating misinformation to its relatively young user base. However, little is known to date about how users perceive misinformation or about how platform interventions could be deployed to stop its spread. Two experiments examined users’ perceptions of TikTok videos making claims about a current health issue (monkeypox). Study 1 tested the impact of information type (true vs. false) and source (journalist vs. influencer) on users’ perceptions of TikTok videos, with party identification as a moderator. Participants rated message credibility and source quality higher for true videos and videos with a journalistic source. Study 2 tested the efficacy of three potential misinformation interventions (a banner label, pre-roll video, and click-through warning) and the role of psychological reactance. There was a main effect of the banner label and public service announcement pre-roll video on perceived message credibility. The interventions had no main effect on source quality, but there was a mediation of the PSA pre-roll and banner label on credibility and quality perceptions through reactance. In both studies, participants had difficulty discerning between true and false claims. Implications for journalists and social media companies are discussed, along with suggestions for future research.

title: Do voting advice applications have durable causal effects? Evidence from concurrent survey and field experiments
authors: Micha Germann, Iulia Cioroianu, Fernando Mendez, Constantinos Djouvas
abstract: Voting advice applications (VAAs) are used by millions of voters, yet their causal effects on political knowledge, preferences, and behavior remain unclear. We present new evidence from two experiments conducted during the 2024 UK General Election: (1) a panel survey experiment that provides access to participants’ VAA advice, achieves high compliance with treatment assignment, and allows us to track outcomes over time; and (2) a concurrent field experiment embedded in a real-world VAA that allows us to assess the ecological validity of our findings. We find that VAA usage leads to durable changes in voters’ perception of how close they are to parties on policy issues, shifts party preferences in line with the advice received, and affects the vote choices of undecided voters. These results suggest that VAAs play an important role in election campaigns. However, we find no evidence that VAAs increase electoral participation.

title: Room for Error: Identifying Question Order Effects in Factual Measures When Meaning or Context Shifts
authors: Daniel Goldstein
abstract: Long-running surveys designed to measure trends face a dilemma of prioritization: making improvements and updates to survey items or maintaining consistent instrumentation across survey waves. This includes the order of questions, as researchers have shown that earlier questions in a survey may affect respondents’ answers to later questions, though inconsistent question order across repeated surveys is underdiscussed as an issue for factual items. Primarily theorized to function through the cognitive response process whereby the prior question(s) frames or provides a context for the latter question(s), this phenomenon is known as question order effects. This article examines an example of a clarification order effect in factual questions where reordering the questions reduces confusion and leads to more valid responses. Using data from three surveys conducted in New York City, we examine the impact of question order on estimates of housing unit size. In two surveys where total residential rooms were asked about before bedrooms, paradata indicated increased respondent confusion relative to asking about bedrooms first. In two surveys where the items either had their order reversed or were reformatted to appear closer together, respondents reported more total rooms on average. Qualitative interviewer feedback suggested that when confronted with a question about rooms without other context, respondents often gave the number of bedrooms in their home. They frequently corrected their response after being asked about bedrooms, though not universally. We suggest that this order effect arose because contemporary respondents think more readily about their unit size in terms of bedrooms than rooms. Our analysis motivates our recommendation that questionnaire designers consider question order alignment with background respondent salience as another tool beyond definitions to help comprehension. Lessons indicate that regular and frequent review of survey items, order, and formatting for potential updates can smooth discontinuities and both improve measurement and maintain continuity.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Using Recordings of Survey Interviews and Machine Learning to Evaluate Differences in Interviewer–Respondent Interactions Between Telephone, In-Person, and Video Interviews
authors: Hanyu Sun, Brad Edwards, Ting Yan
abstract: Computer-Assisted Recorded Interviewing captures audio recordings of survey interviews in real time, producing a distinctive form of unstructured paradata—question-level audio files that capture the question–answer sequences between the interviewer and respondent. These recordings offer insights into the survey response process, enabling a deeper understanding of how responses are formed and delivered. This paper explores the use of machine learning to automate the processing of recordings and to compare interviewer–respondent interactions in video interviews with those of in-person and telephone interviews in the production environment of a large national survey of US households. We first applied machine learning algorithms to transcribe the audio recordings and generate indicators describing interviewer–respondent interactions. We then assessed differences across the three modes in two interviewer behaviors indicative of adherence to standardized interviewing protocol (reading questions verbatim and maintaining question meaning) and in three interaction outcome measures indicative of respondent difficulty answering survey questions (number of the respondent’s turns, duration of the respondent’s first turn, and the total duration of turns with speech). We found significant differences in interviewer question reading behaviors and in the duration of the respondent’s first turn across the three modes, but the differences were small. Additionally, the question itself emerged as the primary source of variability across all outcome measures. This paper demonstrates a viable method for using recordings to efficiently assess interviewer–respondent interactions for research purposes.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Addressing Missing Data From Prompt Noncompliance: A Practical Guide to Auxiliary Variables in Ecological Momentary Assessment
authors: Stefan Schneider, Marta Walentynowicz, Meynard J. Toledo, Raymond Hernandez, Doerte U. Junghaenel, Joshua M. Smyth, Arthur A. Stone
abstract: Missing data from noncompliance and missed prompts are pervasive in ecological-momentary-assessment (EMA) research. Although researchers often examine variables associated with prompt nonresponse, these variables are rarely incorporated into analytic models, leaving standard multilevel analyses to rely on missing-at-random (MAR) assumptions that are often implausible given the available data. In this tutorial, we introduce an accessible strategy for integrating such variables, known as “auxiliary variables,” directly into multilevel models to bolster the plausibility of the MAR assumption. We outline a practical framework for identifying promising auxiliary variables in EMA data sets (e.g., structural-design features, lagged self-reports, passive metadata) and provide step-by-step instructions for (a) preparing EMA data sets, (b) evaluating the utility of candidate auxiliary variables, and (c) incorporating them into multilevel models of EMA data. To facilitate adoption, we supply open-source R code for each step and introduce an R function ( EMAuxiliary ) that streamlines the estimation of multilevel models with auxiliary variables using freely available Blimp software. A fully worked example using real EMA data illustrates the approach. Our aim is to equip applied researchers with a practical, widely applicable method for reducing bias from missing prompts and strengthening inferences in EMA studies.
journal_full: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

title: Prediction-Based Adaptive Designs for Reducing Wave Nonresponse Rates and Bias in Panel Surveys
authors: John Collins, Saskia Bartholomäus, Tobias Gummer, Bernd Weiß, Christoph Kern
abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based nonresponse prediction in panel surveys enables selective interventions. However, the optimal use of ML predictions in Adaptive Survey Design (ASD) remains uncertain. We propose a method that integrates field experiment results on incentives, questionnaire length, and questionnaire content with ML-based propensity models to simulate ASD strategies ex-post with minimal assumptions. Using German panel data, we show that treating 15 percent of panelists, selected through ML-based predictions and R-indicator analysis, with increased cash incentives or a survey module on the respondents’ preferred topic can reduce nonresponse rates by up to 2 percentage points. These strategies also reduced bias in selected variables. We present our method as a framework for survey researchers to evaluate the expected outcomes of multiple ASD regimes simultaneously in a realistic setting. The framework helps identify both the criteria for allocating treatments to specific participant groups and the most effective modifications to the survey protocol.

title: How Model Choice and Memory Shape Preference Consistency in Large Language Models
authors: Yick Chung
abstract: When a language model answers a sequence of questions, researchers report the model and temperature but rarely what or how it was told about its own earlier answers. I show that this underreported setting behaves as a mode effect. Testing four large language model (LLM) families with revealed preference theory (GARP) across moral, economic, and social tasks ( N = 5,926 ), I find that how prior choices re-enter the prompt, the memory condition , moves the share of internally consistent subjects by up to 48 percentage points, mostly where that share starts lowest. Memory also influences which preferences the models express and, in a silicon-sampling extension, it brings the answers closer to the human distribution. Nonetheless, gains in consistency and surface fidelity do not necessarily translate into representativeness: a consistent, human-looking model may not represent any human population. For LLMs as social-science instruments, this study offers promise, caution, and a method for testing the stability of sequential outputs.
